vtrmc-2010-01.title: An explicit integer inverse
vtrmc-2010-01.body:
**Answer: every $n$ with $1\le n\le 100$.**

Write $S_r=I+A+\cdots+A^{r-1}$. Since $(I-A)S_{101}=I-A^{101}$ and $S_{101}=0$, we get $A^{101}=I$. In particular $A$ is invertible with inverse $A^{100}$, an integer matrix, so $\det A\cdot\det A^{100}=1$ with both integers: $\det A=\pm1$.

Fix $1\le n\le100$ and let $r=101-n\in\{1,\dots,100\}$. Then
$$A^n+A^{n+1}+\cdots+A^{100}=A^n S_r ,$$
so it suffices to show $\det S_r=\pm1$.

$101$ is prime (it has no prime factor $\le\sqrt{101}<11$), so there is a positive integer $q$ with $rq\equiv1\pmod{101}$; write $rq=1+101k$ with $k\ge0$. Let $T=I+A^r+A^{2r}+\cdots+A^{(q-1)r}$, an integer matrix. Multiplying out,
$$S_rT=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}A^{ir+j}=\sum_{m=0}^{rq-1}A^m ,$$
since every $m\in\{0,\dots,rq-1\}$ is uniquely $ir+j$. Split the $rq=101k+1$ powers into $k$ blocks of $101$ consecutive powers and one last term:
$$\sum_{m=0}^{rq-1}A^m=\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}A^{101t}S_{101}+A^{101k}=0+I=I .$$
So $S_rT=I$; taking determinants, $\det S_r\cdot\det T=1$ with both factors integers, hence $\det S_r=\pm1$.

Therefore $\det(A^n+\cdots+A^{100})=(\det A)^n\det S_r=\pm1$ for all $1\le n\le100$. ∎

vtrmc-2010-01.title: Eigenvalues and cyclotomic polynomials
vtrmc-2010-01.body:
Every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ (over $\mathbb C$) satisfies $1+\lambda+\cdots+\lambda^{100}=0$, i.e. $\lambda^{101}=1$, $\lambda\ne1$: $\lambda$ is a primitive $101$st root of unity ($101$ is prime). The characteristic polynomial $\chi_A$ has integer coefficients and all its roots are roots of the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{101}(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{100}$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. Hence $\chi_A=\Phi_{101}^{\,m}$ with $d=100m$: each primitive $101$st root $\zeta$ is an eigenvalue of multiplicity exactly $m$.

For a polynomial $p$, the eigenvalues of $p(A)$ with multiplicity are $p(\lambda)$ (triangularise $A$), so $\det p(A)=\prod_\lambda p(\lambda)$. With $p(x)=x^n+\cdots+x^{100}=x^n\frac{1-x^{r}}{1-x}$, $r=101-n$:
$$\det p(A)=\Big(\prod_{\zeta}\zeta^n\cdot\frac{\prod_\zeta(1-\zeta^{r})}{\prod_\zeta(1-\zeta)}\Big)^{m}.$$
Since $\gcd(r,101)=1$, $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^r$ permutes the primitive roots, so the two products over $1-\zeta$ agree. And $\prod_\zeta\zeta=\Phi_{101}(0)\cdot(-1)^{100}=1$. Hence $\det(A^n+\cdots+A^{100})=1$ for **every** $1\le n\le 100$.

(Check: for the $100\times100$ companion matrix of $\Phi_{101}$ a computer gives determinant $1$ for $n=1,2,50,99,100$.) ∎

vtrmc-2010-02.title: Work mod 16 for exponents, then mod 17
vtrmc-2010-02.body:
Write $F_i=f_i(75)$. Every $F_i$ is a power of $75=3\cdot5^2$, so it is odd and prime to $17$.

**Step 1: $F_i \bmod 16$.** The group of odd residues mod $16$ has exponent $4$ ($x^4\equiv1$ for odd $x$), so for odd $a$ the value $a^a\bmod16$ depends only on $a\bmod16$ (which determines $a\bmod4$). Now $F_1=75\equiv11$, and
$$11^{11}\equiv11^{3}=1331\equiv3,\qquad 3^3=27\equiv11\pmod{16}.$$
By induction, $F_i\equiv11\pmod{16}$ for odd $i$ and $F_i\equiv3\pmod{16}$ for even $i$.

**Step 2: $F_i\bmod17$.** By Fermat, $x^{16}\equiv1\pmod{17}$ for $17\nmid x$, so $F_{i+1}=F_i^{F_i}\equiv F_i^{\,F_i\bmod16}\pmod{17}$. Hence
$$F_{i+2}\equiv F_i^{\,3\cdot11}=F_i^{33}\equiv F_i^{1}\pmod{17}\qquad(i\ge1),$$
because the two exponents used are $11$ and $3$ in some order and $33\equiv1\pmod{16}$. So $F_{100}\equiv F_{98}\equiv\cdots\equiv F_2\pmod{17}$.

**Step 3.** $F_2=75^{75}\equiv7^{75}\equiv7^{11}\pmod{17}$ (as $75\equiv11\pmod{16}$). With $7^2=49\equiv-2$, $7^4\equiv4$, $7^8\equiv16\equiv-1$:
$$7^{11}=7^8\cdot7^2\cdot7\equiv(-1)(-2)(7)=14\pmod{17}.$$

**Answer: $14$.**

vtrmc-2010-02.title: Iterate modulo 272
vtrmc-2010-02.body:
Since $\gcd(75,272)=1$ with $272=16\cdot17$, all $F_i$ are units mod $272$. The unit group mod $272$ has exponent $\operatorname{lcm}(\lambda(16),\lambda(17))=\operatorname{lcm}(4,16)=16$, so $F_{i+1}\bmod 272$ is determined by $F_i\bmod272$ (which gives both the base and the exponent mod $16$):
$$F_{i+1}\equiv \big(F_i\bmod272\big)^{\,F_i\bmod16}\pmod{272}.$$
Iterating this map $99$ times from $75$ (by hand it becomes periodic with period $2$ immediately after the first step, by the argument above; by computer it is instant) gives $F_{100}\equiv14\pmod{17}$.

**Answer: $14$.**

vtrmc-2010-03.title: Sum of the seventh roots of unity
vtrmc-2010-03.body:
$\omega=e^{2\pi i/7}$ satisfies $1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^6=0$; taking real parts,
$$1+2\left(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7+\cos\tfrac{4\pi}7+\cos\tfrac{6\pi}7\right)=0 .$$
Since $\cos\frac{4\pi}7=-\cos\frac{3\pi}7$ and $\cos\frac{6\pi}7=-\cos\frac{\pi}7$, this reads
$$1-2\cos\tfrac{\pi}{7}+2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{7}-2\cos\tfrac{3\pi}{7}=0.\qquad(\ast)$$

**$\cos(\pi/7)$ is a root.** For any $\theta$, with $x=\cos\theta$, $\cos2\theta=2x^2-1$ and $\cos3\theta=4x^3-3x$, so
$$1-2\cos\theta+2\cos2\theta-2\cos3\theta=1-2x+4x^2-2-8x^3+6x=-(8x^3-4x^2-4x+1).$$
By $(\ast)$ with $\theta=\pi/7$, $x=\cos\frac\pi7$ is a root.

**$\cos(3\pi/7)$ is a root.** With $\theta=3\pi/7$: $\cos\frac{6\pi}7=-\cos\frac\pi7$ and $\cos\frac{9\pi}7=\cos\frac{5\pi}7=-\cos\frac{2\pi}7$, so
$$1-2\cos\tfrac{3\pi}7+2\cos\tfrac{6\pi}7-2\cos\tfrac{9\pi}7=1-2\cos\tfrac{3\pi}7-2\cos\tfrac{\pi}7+2\cos\tfrac{2\pi}7=0$$
by $(\ast)$. Hence $\cos\frac{3\pi}7$ is also a root.

**The third root.** By Vieta the roots sum to $\frac48=\frac12$, and $(\ast)$ says $\cos\frac\pi7+\cos\frac{3\pi}7-\cos\frac{2\pi}7=\frac12$. So the third root is $-\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}$ $(=\cos\frac{5\pi}7)$. These three numbers are distinct, so they are all the roots. ∎

**Roots:** $\cos\frac\pi7,\ -\cos\frac{2\pi}7,\ \cos\frac{3\pi}7$.

vtrmc-2010-03.title: Using $\cos4\theta=-\cos3\theta$
vtrmc-2010-03.body:
For $\theta\in\{\frac\pi7,\frac{3\pi}7,\frac{5\pi}7\}$ we have $7\theta\in\{\pi,3\pi,5\pi\}$, so $4\theta=7\theta-3\theta$ gives $\cos4\theta=-\cos3\theta$. With $x=\cos\theta$,
$$0=\cos4\theta+\cos3\theta=(8x^4-8x^2+1)+(4x^3-3x)=8x^4+4x^3-8x^2-3x+1=(x+1)(8x^3-4x^2-4x+1).$$
The three values $\cos\frac\pi7>\cos\frac{3\pi}7>\cos\frac{5\pi}7$ are distinct and different from $-1$, so they are three distinct roots of the cubic $8x^3-4x^2-4x+1$, hence all of its roots. Since $\cos\frac{5\pi}7=-\cos\frac{2\pi}7$, the other two roots are $\cos\frac{3\pi}7$ and $-\cos\frac{2\pi}7$. ∎

vtrmc-2010-04.title: Similar triangles (official idea)
vtrmc-2010-04.body:
Since $A+B+C=180^\circ$, we have $3A+3B+3C=540^\circ=4A+3C$, so $A=3B$. Then $4B=A+B<180^\circ$, so $B<45^\circ$, and $A>B$ gives $a>b$.

**Point $D$.** Let $D$ be the point on segment $BC$ with $CD=\frac{b^2}{a}$ (possible as $\frac{b^2}a<a$). Then $\frac{CD}{CA}=\frac{CA}{CB}$ and triangles $CDA$, $CAB$ share the angle at $C$, so $\triangle CDA\sim\triangle CAB$. Hence $\angle CDA=\angle CAB=3B$ and $\frac{AD}{AB}=\frac{CA}{CB}$, i.e. $AD=\frac{bc}{a}$. Also $BD=a-\frac{b^2}{a}$.

In triangle $ABD$: $\angle ABD=B$, $\angle ADB=180^\circ-3B$, hence $\angle BAD=2B$.

**Point $E$.** Since $\angle BAD=2B>B$, the ray from $A$ inside angle $BAD$ making angle $B$ with $AB$ meets segment $BD$ at a point $E$. Triangle $ABE$ has two angles equal to $B$, so $BE=AE$. In triangle $AED$: $\angle EAD=2B-B=B$, $\angle ADE=180^\circ-3B$, so $\angle AED=2B$.

Triangles $ABD$ and $EAD$ have angles $(B,2B,180^\circ-3B)$ at $(B,A,D)$ and $(A,E,D)$ respectively, so $\triangle BAD\sim\triangle AED$ and
$$\frac{BD}{AD}=\frac{AD}{ED}=\frac{AB}{AE}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad ED=\frac{AD^2}{BD},\ \ AE=\frac{AB\cdot AD}{BD}.$$
From $BE=BD-ED$ and $BE=AE$: $BD-\frac{AD^2}{BD}=\frac{AB\cdot AD}{BD}$, i.e. $BD^2=AD^2+AB\cdot AD$.

**Conclusion.** Substituting $BD=a-\frac{b^2}a$, $AD=\frac{bc}a$, $AB=c$ and multiplying by $a^2$:
$$(a^2-b^2)^2=b^2c^2+abc^2=bc^2(a+b).$$
Dividing by $a+b>0$ gives $(a-b)^2(a+b)=bc^2$. ∎

vtrmc-2010-04.title: Law of sines
vtrmc-2010-04.body:
As before $A=3B$, so $C=180^\circ-4B$ and $\sin C=\sin4B$. By the law of sines, $a=2R\sin3B$, $b=2R\sin B$, $c=2R\sin4B$; both sides of the claim are homogeneous of degree $3$, so it suffices to prove
$$(\sin3B-\sin B)^2(\sin3B+\sin B)=\sin B\,\sin^24B .$$
By sum-to-product, $\sin3B-\sin B=2\cos2B\sin B$ and $\sin3B+\sin B=2\sin2B\cos B=4\sin B\cos^2B$. So the left side is
$$4\cos^22B\sin^2B\cdot4\sin B\cos^2B=16\sin^3B\cos^2B\cos^22B .$$
The right side is $\sin B\,(2\sin2B\cos2B)^2=\sin B\cdot4\cdot4\sin^2B\cos^2B\cos^22B=16\sin^3B\cos^2B\cos^22B$. They agree. ∎

vtrmc-2010-05.title: Parametrise the deltoid and use Green's theorem
vtrmc-2010-05.body:
Put the centre $X$ of $A$ at the origin and $P=(3,0)$. Let $\theta$ be the angle of the contact point $Z$ of the two circles, so $Z=3(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and the centre of $B$ is $Y=2(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$.

**Rolling without slipping.** The arc of $A$ from $P$ to $Z$ (length $3\theta$) equals the arc of $B$ from $Q$ to $Z$, so $\angle QYZ=3\theta$ (radius $1$). The direction of $\overrightarrow{YZ}$ is $\theta$; rolling inside, $Q$ lags behind, so $\overrightarrow{YQ}$ has direction $\theta-3\theta=-2\theta$. Therefore
$$Q(\theta)=\big(2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta,\ 2\sin\theta-\sin2\theta\big),\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi,$$
with $Q(0)=P$. Rolling once round means $\theta$ runs from $0$ to $2\pi$. This curve is the deltoid (three cusps, at $\theta=0,\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{4\pi}3$, where $Q$ touches $A$); it is a simple closed curve traced counterclockwise.

**Area.** By Green's theorem the area is $\frac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. With $x'=-2\sin\theta-2\sin2\theta$ and $y'=2\cos\theta-2\cos2\theta$,
$$xy'-yx'=4\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta-2(\cos^22\theta+\sin^22\theta)-2(\cos\theta\cos2\theta-\sin\theta\sin2\theta)=2-2\cos3\theta .$$
So
$$\text{Area}=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(2-2\cos3\theta)\,d\theta=\frac12\cdot4\pi=2\pi .$$

The official solution computes the same area as $2\int y\,\frac{dx}{d\theta}\,d\theta$ over the upper half (using the symmetry in the $x$-axis), also getting $2\pi$.

**Answer: $2\pi$.**

vtrmc-2010-06.title: Reciprocals have increments tending to 1/2
vtrmc-2010-06.body:
**$a_n\downarrow0$.** The recursion is $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}\left(1-\frac{a_n}2\right)$. By induction $0<a_{n+1}<a_n\le1$: this holds for $n=1$, and if $0<a_{n+1}<a_n\le1$ then $\frac12\le1-\frac{a_n}2<1$, so $0<a_{n+2}<a_{n+1}$. A decreasing positive sequence has a limit $z\in[0,1)$, and passing to the limit gives $z=z(1-\frac z2)$, so $z=0$.

**Reciprocals.** Put $b_n=\frac1{a_n}$. Then $b_{n+2}=\dfrac{b_{n+1}}{1-a_n/2}$, so
$$b_{n+2}-b_{n+1}=b_{n+1}\cdot\frac{a_n/2}{1-a_n/2}=\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\cdot\frac{1}{2-a_n}.$$
For $n\ge2$, $\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}=1-\frac{a_{n-1}}{2}$, hence
$$d_n:=b_{n+2}-b_{n+1}=\frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{a_{n-1}}2\right)(2-a_n)}\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{1}{1\cdot2}=\frac12 \qquad(n\to\infty).$$

**Cesàro.** Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $M\ge2$ with $|d_n-\frac12|<\varepsilon$ for $n\ge M$. For $N>M+1$, telescoping gives $b_N=b_{M+1}+\sum_{n=M}^{N-2}d_n$ (a sum of $N-M-1$ terms), so
$$\frac{b_N}{N}-\frac12=\frac{b_{M+1}-\frac{M+1}2+\sum_{n=M}^{N-2}\left(d_n-\frac12\right)}{N},\qquad\left|\frac{b_N}{N}-\frac12\right|\le\frac{b_{M+1}+\frac{M+1}2}{N}+\varepsilon .$$
The first term tends to $0$, so $\limsup\left|\frac{b_N}N-\frac12\right|\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$, i.e. $\frac{b_N}{N}\to\frac12$. Therefore
$$na_n=\frac{n}{b_n}\longrightarrow2 .$$

(Numerically, $n a_n\approx1.99994$ for $n=10^6$.)

**Answer: $2$.**

vtrmc-2010-07.title: Compare with the second half of each block
vtrmc-2010-07.body:
Let $S=\sum a_n<\infty$ and $B_N=b_1+\cdots+b_N$. All terms are positive, so it suffices to bound the partial sums of $\sum N/B_N$.

**Step 1 (drop the weights).** For $k\le N$, $b_k=\frac{1}{ka_k^2}\ge\frac{1}{Na_k^2}$. Let $m=\lceil N/2\rceil$ and let $W_N=\{N-m+1,\dots,N\}$ be the last $m$ indices up to $N$. Then
$$B_N\ge\frac1N\sum_{k\in W_N}\frac1{a_k^2}.$$

**Step 2 (Cauchy–Schwarz).** For positive $x_1,\dots,x_m$: $m^2\le\left(\sum x_k\right)\left(\sum\frac1{x_k}\right)$ and $\left(\sum\frac1{x_k}\right)^2\le m\sum\frac1{x_k^2}$. Hence $\sum\frac1{x_k^2}\ge\frac{m^3}{(\sum x_k)^2}$. With $T_N=\sum_{k\in W_N}a_k$,
$$B_N\ge\frac{m^3}{N\,T_N^2},\qquad\frac{N}{B_N}\le\frac{N^2T_N^2}{m^3}\le\frac{8\,T_N^2}{N}\le\frac{8S\,T_N}{N},$$
using $m\ge N/2$ and $T_N\le S$.

**Step 3 (swap the order of summation).** 
$$\sum_{N\ge1}\frac{T_N}{N}=\sum_{N\ge1}\frac1N\sum_{k\in W_N}a_k=\sum_{k\ge1}a_k\sum_{N:\,k\in W_N}\frac1N .$$
If $k\in W_N$ then $k\le N$ and $k\ge N-m+1\ge N-\frac{N+1}2+1=\frac{N+1}2$, so $k\le N\le 2k-1$. Thus the inner sum has at most $k$ terms, each $\le\frac1k$, and is $\le1$. Hence $\sum_N\frac{T_N}{N}\le S$.

**Conclusion.**
$$\sum_{N=1}^\infty\frac{N}{b_1+\cdots+b_N}\le 8S\sum_{N}\frac{T_N}N\le 8S^2<\infty .$$
∎

*(The official solution also starts from Step 1 in the form $\frac{n}{B_n}\le\frac{n^2}{a_1^{-2}+\cdots+a_n^{-2}}$, but then assumes $(a_n)$ decreasing; the block argument above avoids that assumption.)*
